content: Pericarditis is a medical condition characterized by inflammation of the pericardium, the sac-like structure that surrounds the heart. This inflammation can lead to symptoms such as chest pain, which often worsens with deep breathing or lying flat. The pericardium is a double-walled, conical-shaped fibro-serous membrane that encases the heart and the roots of the great vessels. Anatomically, it is located posterior to the sternum, spanning from the second to sixth costal cartilages and the T5-T8 vertebrae. Pericarditis can be classified based on the duration and recurrence of the disease into acute, incessant, recurrent, and chronic forms. Additionally, it can be categorized by etiology into infectious causes (e.g., viral, bacterial, fungal, or parasitic) and non-infectious causes (e.g., autoimmune, neoplastic, metabolic, traumatic, iatrogenic, or drug-related). The pathophysiology of pericarditis involves inflammation of the pericardium, which may be accompanied by fluid accumulation. This fluid can be serous (free-flowing) or fibrinous (thicker, containing proteins, fibrin strands, inflammatory cells, cellular debris, and sometimes bacteria). Vascular congestion of the pericardium is also commonly observed. The myocardium, the heart muscle, may or may not be involved in the inflammatory process. If the myocardium is affected, the condition is termed myopericarditis, which may be associated with elevated levels of cardiac biomarkers such as CK and troponin. Cardiotropic viruses often spread hematogenously to the myocardium and pericardium, causing acute inflammation with infiltration of polymorphonuclear leukocytes and pericardial vascularization. Most patients with viral pericarditis recover completely, though some may experience recurrences or develop constrictive pericarditis, a potentially disabling complication. Bacterial pericarditis can result from contiguous spread of infection within the chest, post-surgical or traumatic inoculation, hematogenous dissemination, or direct penetration due to injury or cardiothoracic surgery. The causes of pericarditis are broadly divided into infectious and non-infectious categories. Infectious causes include bacterial, viral, fungal, and parasitic infections. Non-infectious causes encompass autoimmune diseases, malignancies, metabolic disorders, trauma, iatrogenic factors, and drug-related etiologies. Life-threatening causes of pericarditis include acute myocardial infarction, Addisonian crisis, aortic dissection or rupture, blunt or penetrating chest trauma, esophageal or gastric perforation, and myocardial rupture. Common causes include viral infections, bacterial organisms, neoplasms, autoimmune conditions, and renal failure. Differentiating pericarditis from other diseases presenting with chest pain, shortness of breath, and tachypnea is critical. Conditions such as myocardial infarction, pulmonary embolism, congestive heart failure, pneumonia, vasculitis, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) must be considered. The clinical manifestations of pericarditis, such as positional chest pain, can help distinguish it from myocardial infarction. Other differential diagnoses include aortic stenosis, coronary artery vasospasm, esophageal rupture, esophageal spasm, esophagitis, acute gastritis, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and peptic ulcer disease. Pericarditis affects approximately 7 per 100,000 individuals annually, with recurrences occurring in about 30% of patients after the first episode. It is more common in men aged 20 to 50 years but can occur in all age groups. In developed countries, pericarditis is most commonly caused by malignancy or viral infections, often following respiratory infections caused by echovirus or coxsackievirus. In children, adenovirus and coxsackievirus are the most common causes. In developing countries, pericarditis is frequently secondary to tuberculosis or HIV infection. Tuberculous pericarditis, caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is found in approximately 1% of all autopsied TB cases and 1-2% of pulmonary TB cases. Routine screening for pericarditis is not recommended due to insufficient evidence. The natural history of pericarditis is often self-limited, with most patients recovering within 2 weeks to 3 months. However, complications such as significant pericardial effusion or cardiac tamponade may require urgent intervention, including pericardiocentesis. If scarring of the pericardium occurs, leading to constrictive pericarditis, surgical removal of the scar tissue may be necessary. Patients with pericarditis typically present with chest pain that changes with position, cough, fever, breathlessness, and fatigue. Less common symptoms include palpitations, hiccups, odynophagia, fainting, dizziness, and abdominal pain, particularly in children. A thorough physical examination is essential to rule out cardiac tamponade, a dangerous complication of pericarditis. Signs of tamponade include pulsus paradoxus, hypotension, elevated jugular venous pressure, and peripheral edema. Laboratory findings in pericarditis often show elevated non-specific markers of inflammation, such as leukocyte count, C-reactive protein (CRP), and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR). Cardiac troponin levels may be elevated if there is myocardial injury, as seen in myopericarditis. Diagnostic pericardiocentesis and biopsy can help identify underlying infectious or malignant processes. Electrocardiography (ECG) in pericarditis may reveal diminished voltage and electrical alternans in the presence of a large effusion or tamponade. Chest X-rays may show an enlarged, flask-shaped cardiac silhouette in cases of pericardial effusion or tamponade. Pericardial calcification may be noted in constrictive pericarditis. Echocardiography is crucial for assessing pericardial effusion and monitoring its size, as well as confirming clinical suspicion of cardiac tamponade. CT and MRI imaging can provide additional details about pericardial thickening, fluid characteristics, and associated complications, such as tumors or metastases. Management of pericarditis depends on whether the disease course is uncomplicated or complicated. Uncomplicated pericarditis is typically treated with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen for viral or idiopathic cases, and aspirin for post-myocardial infarction pericarditis. Complicated pericarditis, involving effusion or tamponade, may require urgent pericardiocentesis, antibiotics for purulent effusion, and steroids or colchicine for recurrent or refractory cases. Surgical interventions include pericardiocentesis, pericardial window creation, and pericardiectomy. Pericardiocentesis involves aspirating fluid from the pericardium using a needle, which can be both diagnostic and therapeutic. A pericardial window is a surgical procedure to drain accumulated fluid by creating an opening in the pericardium, preventing fluid reaccumulation and cardiac tamponade. Pericardiectomy, or pericardial stripping, involves the surgical removal of the pericardium to relieve constrictive pericarditis or remove calcified, fibrous tissue. This procedure carries significant risks and is typically reserved for patients with severe symptoms unresponsive to medical management.
